Execute the supplied author's code to answer the task questions. Read /code/README.md
and /REPRODUCING.md first. The controller has already provisioned the author's image:
run commands directly inside this container, not through nested Docker. Work in /code;

experimental code, hardcode answers, or use remembered/published results.
If blocked, submit null values for unanswered questions, with evidence of the blocker
and an optional explanation field. Do not invent values to complete the report. If a required
code change is necessary, explain the blocker instead of silently patching it.
Keep every response in English. Tool outputs include controller-owned artifact IDs and
1-based line numbers. Submit each question's value with evidence from THIS execution.
For plots, use view_image on generated raster files or PDF pages; cite the returned

"line_start":2,"line_end":2}]}}. The example number is not an answer.
An existing file reference does not prove correctness; cite actual computed output.

Frozen development lessons:
# Workflow lessons, revision 2, candidate 2

Apply these rules to the current execution, never as task answers.

## First: preserve the scientific experiment

Do not edit, replace, monkeypatch, or bypass any scientific code, loader, dataset,
formula, filter, random seed, or notebook code cell. This applies equally to original
files, new copies, temporary scripts, and in-memory execution. An apparently equivalent
loader or convenient library dataset is still a scientific substitution. Do not make
one to get an answer. Executing unchanged code and saving its outputs is allowed.
If the unchanged computation cannot run with its documented inputs, submit null for
its unanswered questions with the observed blocker. A failed reproduction is preferable
to a plausible answer from a modified experiment. Do not spend calls trying such fixes.

## Use calls on the requested computation

List available instructions, then read them and /REPRODUCING.md. Missing optional
README files must not prevent other reads. Run the documented entry point. The shell
tool accepts only `command`; omit unsupported timeout arguments. Protect embedded
script variables from shell expansion using quoted scripts or quoted heredocs.
For notebooks, execute unchanged cells once into /results, inspect targeted output
cells, then render that saved execution if needed. Do not repeatedly rerun it to read
outputs. Distinguish a renderer failure from a failed scientific calculation. If only presentation prevents execution, use native
tools to execute the author's unchanged code blocks without rendering, preserving
their code, inputs and settings verbatim; record the rendering blocker separately.
Do not rewrite the computation to imitate its output. Check
a failed loader's documented path and available data once, then record the blocker;
do not search the entire filesystem or try alternate internet endpoints offline.

## Verify meaning before reporting

Match each question's metric, population and conditions to the actual generated
output. Similar labels in another table are not enough. Inspect generated figures
for visual questions and verify the mapping from computed values to displayed labels.
Read-only extraction from objects generated by unmodified author code is acceptable;
reimplementing its scientific computation is not. A focused rerun of unchanged code
is allowed only when needed objects cannot otherwise be inspected. Never replace
execution evidence with manuscript prose or a remembered answer.

## Submit a typed answer with evidence

You have twenty model calls, including errors and the final submit_report call.
Reserve the last two for checking evidence and submitting; stop optional rendering
repairs and repetitive searches before they consume those calls. For numeric questions,
`value` must be a JSON number on the requested scale, with no appended units or prose.
Keep explanations in the explanation field. Retain text or list values when explicitly
requested. Every non-null answer must be supported by this execution of unchanged
scientific code. Otherwise submit null and the observed reason, without fabricating
or repairing the result.

40: knitr::opts_chunk$set(include = FALSE) # This option stops the code chunks from being output from the knit.
41: ```
42: 
43: ```{r load_packages}
44: library(meta) # For meta-analyses and forest plots.
45: library(irr) # For inter-rater agreement
46: library(knitr) # For kable function.
47: library(kableExtra) # For kable table styling.
48: library(english) # To convert numbers to word equivalents via words(). 
49: library(boot) # For inv.logit() function.
50: library(tidyverse) # For cleaner code.
51: ```
52: ```{r function_metaDisc}
53: # For running meta-analyses on proportions (most of the meta analyses in this review).
54: 
55: metaDisc <- function(df){
56:   # initialize a dataframe to hold all 40 meta-analytic estimates, CIs, PIs, and number of articles analyzed.
57:   estim <- data.frame(matrix(ncol = 7, nrow = length(df)))
58:   colnames(estim) <- c("b", "lower.random", "upper.random", "lower.predict", "upper.predict", "k", "n")
59:   
60:   # assign the colnames from df to the rownames for estim so that the results line up in the next section of code
61:   rownames(estim) <- colnames(df)
62:   
63:   # initialize lists of lists to hold the results of the 40 meta-analyses
64:   metaList<-list()
65:   
66:   # calculate the meta-analytic estimates, CIs, PIs, and number of articles analyzed for outcomes from prospectively registered studies
67:   for (i in grep("discProAny", colnames(df)):grep("discProTime", colnames(df))){
68:     if (sum(!is.na(df[,i] > 0 ))){
69:       # create temporary dataframe with the NAs removed. This is necessary to align the article author and year with the correct article after running each meta-analysis
70:       dfMeta <- df %>% filter(!is.na(df[,i]))
71:       meta <- meta::metaprop(dfMeta[,i], dfMeta$discProDenom,
72:                           # method for conducting the meta-analytic model (a multi-level regression)
73:                           method="GLMM",
74:                           # method to calculate tau
75:                           method.tau="ML",
76:                           # method to calculate the confidence interval for tau^2 (which we don't report)
77:                           method.tau.ci="J", 
78:                           comb.random=TRUE, 
79:                           prediction=TRUE,
80:                           level.predict=0.95,
81:                           # helpful for meta-analyses of few articles (modifies Student's T-distribution)
82:                           hakn=TRUE
83:       )
84:       # create the study labels for the forest plots
85:       meta$studlab <- paste(dfMeta$author, dfMeta$pubYear)
86:       
87:     metaList[[i]] <- meta #store a list of the meta variable for all 40 meta-analyses to make forest plots later
88:     # All meta-analytic estimates, CIs, and PIs, need to have inv.logit() run on them to reverse the logit() function that is used in the metaprop() function. 
89:     estim[i,] <- c(inv.logit(meta$TE.random), 
90:                    inv.logit(meta$lower.random), 
91:                    inv.logit(meta$upper.random),
92:                    inv.logit(meta$lower.predict),
93:                    inv.logit(meta$upper.predict),
94:                    meta$k,
95:                    sum(meta$data[,2]))
96:         }
97:   }
98:   
99:   # same as above for outcomes from studies with unclear timing of registration.
100:   for (i in grep("discAny", colnames(df)):grep("discTime", colnames(df))){
101:     if (sum(!is.na(df[,i] > 0 ))){
102:       
103:       # create temporary dataframe with the NAs removed
104:       dfMeta <- df %>% filter(!is.na(df[,i]))
105:       meta <- meta::metaprop(dfMeta[,i], dfMeta$discDenom,
106:                              method="GLMM", 
107:                              method.tau="ML", 
108:                              method.tau.ci="J", 
109:                              comb.random=TRUE, 
110:                              prediction=TRUE,
111:                              level.predict=0.95,
112:                              hakn=TRUE
113:       )
114:       meta$studlab <- paste(dfMeta$author, dfMeta$pubYear)
115:       
116:       metaList[[i]] <- meta # store a list of the meta variable for all 40 meta-analyses to make forest plots later
117:       estim[i,] <- c(inv.logit(meta$TE.random), 
118:                      inv.logit(meta$lower.random), 
119:                      inv.logit(meta$upper.random),
120:                      inv.logit(meta$lower.predict),
121:                      inv.logit(meta$upper.predict),
122:                      meta$k,
123:                      sum(meta$data[,2]))
124:     }
125:   }
126:       
127: 
128:   # same as above for non-outcome discrepancies for both prospectively and unclear timing of registration articles
129:   # Increment by 2 because we have a denominator for each non-outcome discrepancy in the column after the numerator. This is also the reason this block of code needs to be separate from the outcome discrepancies, which all share a denominator.
130:   for (i in seq(from = grep("discProOtherElig", colnames(df))[1], to = grep("discOtherResults", colnames(df))[1], by = 2)) {
131:     if (sum(!is.na(df[,i] > 0 ))){
132:       # create temporary dataframe with the NAs removed
133:       dfMeta <- df %>% filter(!is.na(df[,i]))
134:       meta <- meta::metaprop(dfMeta[,i], dfMeta[,i+1],
135:                              method="GLMM", 
136:                              method.tau="ML", 
137:                              method.tau.ci="J", 
138:                              comb.random=TRUE, 
139:                              prediction=TRUE,
140:                              level.predict=0.95,
141:                              hakn=TRUE
142:       )
143:       meta$studlab <- paste(dfMeta$author, dfMeta$pubYear)
144:       
145:       metaList[[i]] <- meta # store a list of the meta variable for all 40 meta-analyses to make forest plots later
146:       estim[i,] <- c(inv.logit(meta$TE.random), 
147:                      inv.logit(meta$lower.random), 
148:                      inv.logit(meta$upper.random),
149:                      inv.logit(meta$lower.predict),
150:                      inv.logit(meta$upper.predict),
151:                      meta$k,
152:                      sum(meta$data[,2]))
153:     }
154:   }
155:       
156: 
157:   return(list(estim, metaList))
158: }
159: 
160: ```

162: ```{r function_metaRR}
163: # For running meta-analyses on Risk Ratios (i.e., likelihood ratios). For the exploratory analyses.
164: 
165: metaRR <- function(Ee, Ne, Ec, Nc, df){
166:   
167:   
168:   meta <- meta::metabin(Ee, Ne, Ec, Nc,
169:                        # Risk ratio analysis will not take the parameters below that I used in the other analyses. Instead, they default to method = "MH" and method.tau = "DL"
170:                        # method="GLMM", 
171:                        # method.tau="ML", 
172:                        # method.tau.ci="J", 
173:                         comb.random=TRUE, 
174:                         prediction=TRUE,
175:                         level.predict=0.95,
176:                         hakn=TRUE,
177:                         sm = "RR"
178:   )
179:   
180:     meta$studlab <- paste(df$author, df$pubYear)
181:     
182:     CI <- paste0(round(exp(meta$lower.random),2), "-", round(exp(meta$upper.random),2))  
183:     
184:     #sprintf() is necessary to keep trailing zeros on a PI that = 1.00
185:     PI <- paste0(round(exp(meta$lower.predict),2), "-", sprintf("%.2f", round(exp(meta$upper.predict),3)))
186:                
187:                  
188:   return(list(meta, CI, PI))
189: }
190: ```
191: 
192: ```{r function_makeCI}
193: # To format the confidence intervals in the tables.
194: makeCI <- function(data){
195: 
196:   data <- round(data, 2)
197:   CI <- paste0(data$lower.random*100, "-", data$upper.random*100, "%")
198:   return(CI)
199:   
200:   }
201: ```
202: 
203: ```{r function_makePI}
204: # To format the prediction intervals in the tables.
205: makePI <- function(data){
206:   
207:   data[,1:5] <- data[,1:5]*100
208:   
209:   for (i in 1:nrow(data)){
210:     data[i,4] <- ifelse(data[i,4] < 0.5, signif(data[i,4],1), round(data[i,4],0))
211:     data[i,5] <- ifelse(data[i,5] > 99.5, signif(data[i,5] - 100, 1) + 100, round(data[i,5],0))
212:   }
213:   
214:   PI <- paste0(data$lower.predict, "-", data$upper.predict, "%")
215:   return(PI)
216:   
217:   }
218: ```
219: 
220: 
221: ```{r clean_screening_data}
222: # Import the screening data. Calculate the number of articles in each category. Calculate inter-rater reliability
223: screen <- read.csv("/data/preregSR_dataScreen.csv", header = TRUE)
224: 
225: # Calculate Cohen's kappa for whether articles were marked (1) relevant to systematic or not, and (2) relevant to the scoping review or not. I am doing this as two kappa values for binary variables.
226: screen <- screen %>%  mutate(RCsr = ifelse((RC == "BOTH" | RC == "SR"), 1, 0))
